title: Setting Up the Command-Line Environment
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter sets up the working environment the rest of the course assumes: a UNIX-style command line, Git for version control, SSH for reaching a remote machine, and a proper text editor. It is deliberately thin on UNIX itself — the lecture points to an external tutorial for that and does a short demo in class rather than teaching the shell from the page — but it does lay out what each tool is for, the handful of commands used daily, and a short list of things worth knowing about your own machine before you start relying on it. It assumes you have used a computer before, not that you have used a command line. ## Working on UNIX "UNIX" here means any UNIX-like operating system, including Linux and macOS. Most modern scientific computing is done on UNIX-based machines, often by remotely logging in to a UNIX-based server rather than working on the machine in front of you. There are several ways to get access to a UNIX-style command line environment — a Mac's built-in terminal, a Linux machine, or an account on a remote server — and the course does not re-teach the shell itself here: it relies on a separate tutorial on the basics of UNIX (and, in earlier iterations, on a "Computing Skills Workshop" run the week before term). If the command line is already familiar, that tutorial can be skipped; if not, the expectation is to work through it before the second class, with a section meeting available to ask questions of the GSI and other students. An alternative introduction, which also previews the shell-scripting material covered later in the course, is the Software Carpentry shell tutorial. ## Parts of a computer, and where the bottleneck is The course does not dwell on hardware, but a few components matter for writing effective code: - the **CPU**, which does the actual computation, backed by a small amount of very fast **cache** memory sitting close to it; - **main memory (RAM)**, connected to the CPU by a **bus**; - **disk**, for persistent storage. The reason this list matters is that the slow step in a computation can be any one of three different things, depending on what the code is doing: the calculations themselves on the CPU, moving data back and forth between RAM and the CPU, or reading and writing data to and from disk. Which one is the bottleneck changes what "making it faster" means for a given piece of code, which is why it is worth having the picture in mind early rather than discovering it by trial and error later in the course. A more detailed treatment of this, including how programs actually run, is left to an outside overview from a comparable course at CMU — the lecture flags it as useful without reproducing it. ## Version control with Git Version control is the practice of keeping track of changes made to files on a computer over time — most often code, but any text file. It works particularly well for text because version control tools track *differences* between two versions of a file on a line-by-line basis. It is described as a central practice in modern scientific computing, and the course uses Git for it throughout: for accessing course materials, submitting problem sets, and the final project. Git stores the files for a project in a **repository**. Two commands cover most of what is needed to follow along with the class materials from the command line: ```bash # clone (copy) a repository from GitHub git clone https://github.com/berkeley-stat243/fall-2026 # update a local copy to reflect changes made remotely cd /any/directory/inside/the/local/repository git pull ``` Graphical front ends to Git exist too — GitHub Desktop is mentioned as a reasonable one for Mac and Windows — but the course leans on the command line. Section/lab sessions go further: setting up a repository from scratch, making changes, and working with local and remote copies side by side. Beyond the two commands above, the material points to an external tutorial on the basics of Git, and (in an earlier iteration) to further tutorials on Git for working scientists and on branching. ## Connecting to and moving files between machines Reaching a remote UNIX machine is done with **SSH** — available as the `ssh` command on the UNIX command line, with equivalent clients on Windows. Connecting without typing a password each time is possible too, via SSH keys. A connection to a remote server looks like: ```bash ssh username@remotehost.berkeley.edu ``` Moving files between machines uses **scp**, which takes options similar to `cp`. To copy a local file to a remote machine: ```bash scp file.txt username@remotehost.berkeley.edu:~/research/. ``` and to copy a file from the remote machine back to the one you are on: ```bash scp username@remotehost.berkeley.edu:/data/file.txt ~/research/renamed.txt ``` One detail that trips people up: relative paths make sense for locations on the local machine, but on the remote machine every path either has to be absolute or relative to your home directory there — there is no shared notion of "current directory" spanning the two machines. Graphical file transfer clients exist as an alternative to typing `scp` by hand. ## Knowing your context A recurring theme in working from the shell is that the same command can mean different things depending on state that is easy to lose track of. The questions worth having an automatic answer to, every time you're about to type something into a terminal or run code, are: - What machine am I on? - What user am I? - What is the current working directory? - What Git branch am I on, if the working directory is inside a Git repository? - What Conda environment am I in, if relevant? None of these are hard to check individually, but the failure mode is not checking — running the right command in the wrong directory, on the wrong machine, or in the wrong environment. ## Editors Scientific computing calls for a **text editor**, not a word processor. Code files, plain-text data files, and markup documents (Markdown, Quarto, R Markdown, LaTeX) are all plain text underneath, and a word processor's formatting actively gets in the way of that. The rule stated plainly in the material: don't use Microsoft Word or Google Docs to edit code files or Markdown/Quarto/R Markdown/LaTeX. A rough map of the options: - traditional editors that originated on UNIX: **emacs**, **vim**; - more recent general editors: **Sublime Text** (proprietary); - Windows-specific: **WinEdt**, **Notepad++**; - Mac-specific: **Aquamacs Emacs**, **TextMate**, **TextEdit**; - **RStudio** bundles a built-in editor for R and Quarto/R Markdown files as part of a larger IDE — Python code chunks can also be edited and run inside it; - **VS Code** is an IDE with a code editor customized for many languages, Jupyter notebooks, and Quarto documents, and built-in AI assistance through GitHub Copilot (free with GitHub Education). It's fine to start with something as basic as Notepad, but worth the time over the first few weeks to move to something more capable — it pays off over the rest of a graduate career. One Windows specific trap: file suffixes are often hidden by default, which can silently turn `file.txt` edited as "just text" into something else. ### Basic emacs Emacs has dedicated modes for different file types (Python, R, C, LaTeX, ...), and setting these up for the languages you use regularly is worth the initial effort. Working in Python or R, you can start an interpreter in a separate Emacs buffer and send code to it directly, seeing the results without leaving the editor; for R specifically, ESS ("Emacs Speaks Statistics") mode helps, and comes built into Aquamacs Emacs. When tunnelling a graphical Emacs window through SSH is slow or impossible, opening Emacs directly in the terminal avoids the problem: ```bash emacs -nw file.txt ``` A few key bindings worth knowing (several of these — `Ctrl-a`, `Ctrl-e`, `Ctrl-k`, `Ctrl-y` — also work at the command line and inside interactive Python and R sessions): | Sequence | Result | |---|---| | `Ctrl-x, Ctrl-c` | Close the file | | `Ctrl-x, Ctrl-s` | Save the file | | `Ctrl-x, Ctrl-w` | Save with a new name | | `Ctrl-s` | Search | | `Esc` | Get out of the command buffer at the bottom of the screen | | `Ctrl-a` | Go to the beginning of the line | | `Ctrl-e` | Go to the end of the line | | `Ctrl-k` | Delete the rest of the line, forward from the cursor | | `Ctrl-space`, then move | Highlight a block of text | | `Ctrl-w` | Remove the highlighted block into the kill buffer | | `Ctrl-y` (after `Ctrl-k` or `Ctrl-w`) | Paste ("yank") from the kill buffer | ### Basic vim vim is worth knowing even if it isn't your primary editor, because it shows up whether you choose it or not: running `git commit` without the `-m` flag drops you into a vim window by default (this can be changed, but it's useful to be able to escape it without changing anything). vim has two modes. **Normal** mode is for operations — navigating, saving, moving and deleting lines. **Insert** mode is for typing text. Press `i` to go from normal to insert mode, and `Esc` to return to normal mode. From normal mode: `:w` saves, `:x` saves and exits, `:q` exits. Searching a document is `/` followed by the search string and Enter (e.g. `/python docstring`); `Esc` leaves the search. ## Sources - **berkeley-stat243, unit 1 ("UNIX command line basics" / "Version control" / "Connecting to other machines" / "Editors")**, taken primarily from the **fall-2026** iteration — `01-1-unix-command-line-basics.md`, `02-2-version-control.md`, `03-4-connecting-to-other-machines.md` (including its "Knowing your context" section), and `04-6-background-editors.md` — used as the clearest and most current treatment. Licensed CC BY 4.0, converted losslessly from `units/unit1-intro.qmd`. - Cross-checked against the near-identical **fall-2024** and **fall-2025** iterations of the same unit (`01-1-unix-command-line-basics.md`, `02-2-version-control.md`, `03-4-connecting-to-other-machines.md`, `04-5-editors.md` in each), which differ only in small updates (e.g. the fall-2024 editor list omits VS Code's Copilot integration and Notepad++, and neither has the "Knowing your context" section). - **stat243-fall-2021, "Unit 1: Basics of UNIX"** (`01-unit-1-basics-of-unix.md`, `02-2-version-control.md`, `03-4-editors.md`) supplied a small amount of material not carried into later years — the reminder that Mac users can reach a UNIX terminal via Applications → Utilities → Terminal, the suggestion to install the Xcode developer tools on a personal Mac, and pointers to further Git tutorials ("Git for Scientists", Gitwash, and an interactive branching demo). This source is a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer (CC0-1.0, fidelity "reconstructed"), so it is used here only for these small, easily-checked factual details, not for anything more load-bearing. - **Referred to by the lecture material but not contained in it**, and not reproduced here: the course's own UNIX-basics tutorial, the Software Carpentry shell-novice tutorial, the annual "Computing Skills Workshop," a computer-architecture overview from a comparable course at CMU (`36-750.github.io/tools/computer-architecture`), a basics-of-Git tutorial, and the SCF's pages on SSH, SSH keys, and copying files. - No slides or lecture transcript were supplied for this unit — the source is the course's own written unit notes across four year-iterations — and no problem set questions were supplied for it, so there is no Exercises section.
